title: Parallel Omnidirectional Atom Rearrangement with Dynamic Holograms
authors: Samuel A. Engel, Dewei Gong, Ziguang Lin, Lysander Christakis, Kang-Kuen Ni, Norman Y. Yao
abstract: The ability to assemble and reconfigure individual atoms is central to performing quantum science using optical tweezer arrays. Here, we demonstrate parallel omnidirectional atom transport and rearrangement using dynamic holograms generated by a single kilohertz-rate spatial light modulator. By carefully characterizing survival and heating, we show that atoms remain confined even when successive holograms are commanded before the liquid crystal has settled, enabling significantly faster transport. To generate holograms in real time, we develop and implement a warm-start, weighted Gerchberg-Saxton algorithm that achieves performance comparable to neural-network methods without requiring any training. Combining these techniques, we assemble ytterbium atoms into a 2078-site kagome lattice with 99.0% mean filling. In addition, we demonstrate parallel transport between array layers, combining axial and transverse motion to reconfigure atoms in three dimensions. Our approach is readily adaptable to existing tweezer platforms and provides a method for large-scale SLM-based atom assembly as well as programmable three-dimensional control.
summary: This paper presents a method to rapidly and precisely reconfigure arrays of neutral atoms trapped by optical tweezers using dynamic holograms generated by SLMs. By developing a fast, training-free algorithm and exploiting the physics of the liquid crystal response, the authors achieved significantly faster transport and demonstrated programmable, large-scale 3D atom assembly.
main_problem: The central challenge is achieving fast, parallel, and omnidirectional rearrangement of individual neutral atoms trapped in optical tweezer arrays.
main_result: The authors demonstrated significantly faster atom transport by updating the holographic fields faster than the liquid crystal can settle, and achieved high-fidelity assembly of large lattices in 3D.
method: They developed and implemented a warm-start, weighted Gerchberg-Saxton (WGS) algorithm for real-time hologram generation, combined with advanced control protocols like 'overdrive' to accelerate the system response.
model_or_system: The system uses neutral atoms (e.g., Ytterbium) trapped in optical tweezer arrays generated by Liquid-Crystal Spatial Light Modulators (SLMs). The control involves dynamically shaping the light field via holograms to guide atomic movement.
key_observables: Atom survival fraction, heating rate, mean filling fraction (e.g., 99.0%), and maximum transport speed ($v_{	ext{max}}$).
important_parameters: SLM update rate (kilohertz), liquid crystal settle time ($	au_0$), step size ($d$), and transport period ($T$).
main_assumptions: The performance relies on the ability to rapidly update the holographic phase profile and the assumption that the WGS algorithm can accurately model the required light field.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the setup, the assembly of large kagome lattices, and comparative plots showing atom loss/heating rates under different update frequencies ($T > 	au_0$ vs. $T < 	au_0$).
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the need for fast transport, detailing the WGS algorithm for real-time control, demonstrating speed enhancements by beating the LC settling time, and culminating in showing programmable 3D rearrangement capabilities.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the engineering bottleneck in quantum simulation platforms: controlling the physical hardware (SLMs) fast enough to realize the theoretical potential of quantum state manipulation in cold atom arrays.
